narrativeReportMd:
# base64Binary R4->R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`base64Binary` keeps the same datatype identity, but its primitive value regex changed materially. R4's regex was whitespace-tolerant and loose about padding; R6's regex is stricter about base64 syntax and does not allow embedded whitespace, while also allowing the empty lexical value.

## Scope
The local primitive value definition was analyzed. The R6 `PrimitiveType` base class and inherited Element/Extension changes are explicitly out of scope for this datatype report.

## Main migration themes
The main migration issue is lexical normalization. Systems migrating R4 data to R6 should decode and re-encode or otherwise canonicalize base64Binary values, especially values that were line-wrapped, contained whitespace, or used non-canonical padding.

## Highest-impact findings
The single local finding is a value-constraint change on `base64Binary.value`. It can make some R4-valid primitive strings fail R6 validation and can make the R6 empty value difficult to represent in strict R4 validation.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is useful to confirm whether the ballot intended to reject all whitespace in serialized base64Binary values and to decide whether legacy line-wrapped payloads should be normalized automatically or quarantined.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The stricter R6 regex is probably intended to align validation with canonical base64 lexical syntax. A less disruptive transition could have preserved whitespace tolerance with a warning period, but that would keep accepting malformed or ambiguous encodings.

## Follow-up analysis
PrimitiveType/DataType and Element/Extension reports should own the base hierarchy and inherited invariant changes.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `base64Binary` has one local breaking change: the primitive value regex changed from a whitespace-tolerant, permissive R4 pattern to a stricter R6 base64 pattern that also permits an empty value. The top concerns are rejection of line-wrapped legacy payloads, rejection of malformed padding previously accepted by the R4 regex, and R6-to-R4 handling of zero-byte values. The main uncertainty is whether official narrative or ballot notes provide transition guidance beyond the computable regex.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should focus on lexical normalization rather than element remapping. Existing payload bytes can usually be preserved by decoding the R4 string and re-encoding it as canonical base64 without whitespace. Values that matched the old regex only because padding characters appeared in invalid positions need stricter repair or rejection. R6 empty strings should be reviewed when down-converting to R4 because strict R4 regex validation does not accept the empty value.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for the local computable delta because both StructureDefinitions are present and the regex values differ directly on `base64Binary.value`. Confidence is lower for intent and prevalence because no official diff, rendered narrative page, or ballot rationale was used.

findings.title: base64Binary.value regex is stricter about whitespace and padding, but now permits an empty value

oldState.summary: R4 used a whitespace-tolerant regex requiring at least one 4-character group and allowing '=' anywhere in those groups.
oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, the value regex was `(\s*([0-9a-zA-Z\+/=]){4}\s*)+`. This accepted line breaks or other whitespace around each 4-character block and, because `=` was included in the general character class, did not enforce padding only at the end.

newState.summary: R6 uses a stricter base64 regex with no whitespace and padding only in final 2== or 3= form; the whole expression can also match the empty string.
newState.narrativeMd: In R6, the value regex is `(?:[A-Za-z0-9+/]{4})*(?:[A-Za-z0-9+/]{2}==|[A-Za-z0-9+/]{3}=)?`. It permits only base64 alphabet characters and terminal padding, with no whitespace. Because both groups are repeat/optional, an empty lexical value also matches.

facts.note: R6 removes whitespace tolerance and enforces terminal padding shapes, but the new expression also accepts the empty string.
Line-wrapped or pretty-printed base64 strings can be old-valid/new-invalid.

facts.oldValue: Not matched by the R4 regex because of the trailing + quantifier
facts.newValue: Matched by the R6 regex because both groups can occur zero times
facts.note: This creates an R6-to-R4 representability risk for zero-byte payloads serialized as an empty string.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements have the same id and path, `base64Binary.value`, and the same primitive FHIR type extension value `base64Binary`; only the regex extension value changed materially.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation change for the primitive lexical value. An R4 instance containing a line-wrapped base64Binary value, such as a payload with a newline between 4-character groups, can satisfy the R4 regex and fail the R6 regex. Values with non-terminal `=` padding that slipped through R4 regex validation can also fail R6. In the reverse direction, an R6 empty value is accepted by the R6 regex but not by the R4 regex. Runtime risk is medium because many APIs decode base64 before validation or normalize it on serialization, but strict validators, generated regex checks, import pipelines, and schema-derived tests can observe the break.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The datatype is commonly used for attachments, signatures, binary payloads, and encoded content. Rejection or unintended alteration of payload values can block document exchange or corrupt binary evidence if migration tooling strips or repairs content incorrectly.

justification.inferredGoal: Tighten the computable lexical definition of base64Binary to reject non-canonical or malformed base64 and represent zero-length byte streams.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Allow R4-style whitespace around base64 quanta during an R6 transition, while enforcing terminal padding and recommending canonical no-whitespace serialization.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal inferred from the regex is reasonable: align `base64Binary` with a tighter base64 lexical form, reject non-terminal padding, and allow zero-length byte streams. A less-breaking rule could cover line-wrapped R4 values, but preserving all R4 regex matches would also preserve plainly malformed padding, which would undercut the validation goal. Because the viable compatibility path is incomplete and carries interoperability and comparison costs, the break is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would have accepted canonical R6 base64 plus R4-style insignificant whitespace around complete base64 groups, possibly with narrative or warning-level guidance that producers emit canonical no-whitespace values. That would preserve many legacy R4 payloads without structural migration, but it would leave duplicate lexical representations for the same bytes, complicate signature/canonicalization and string comparison behavior, and still would need to reject R4 values whose only validity came from loose `=` placement. Conversion tooling or extensions are mitigations, not base-design alternatives.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would save common line-wrapped payloads, but it would not preserve malformed padding and would keep multiple lexical encodings for the same bytes in base R6 validation.

evidence.detail: R4 base64Binary.value regex permits whitespace and requires one or more 4-character groups.
R6 base64Binary.value regex removes whitespace tolerance, constrains padding position, and can match an empty value.
The value element cardinality remains 0..1 and its underlying FHIRPath type remains System.String, so the material local change is the regex value constraint rather than a type or cardinality change.
R6 retains the same value element cardinality and FHIRPath type while changing the regex extension.

A line-wrapped value such as `QUJD\nRA==` matches the R4 pattern as two whitespace-separated 4-character groups but does not match the R6 pattern because whitespace is absent from the R6 character classes.

examples.examplesMd: The example `data` property is an illustrative host element with datatype `base64Binary`, not a complete resource. `QUJD\nRA==` represents a line-wrapped R4 lexical form that should be normalized to `QUJDRA==` for R6. The empty string example illustrates the regex-level R6-to-R4 issue for a zero-byte payload.

findings.narrativeMd: `base64Binary.value` changed from a permissive R4 lexical pattern to a stricter R6 pattern. Existing R4 data that stored base64 in wrapped lines, included spaces between groups, or used padding forms the R4 regex did not reject can now fail R6 validation even though the element name, cardinality, and primitive datatype identity are unchanged. This can surprise implementers because the semantic definition, "A stream of bytes," looks stable; the break is in the computable regex used by validators and generated parsers.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid values containing whitespace around 4-character groups can become R6-invalid. Values with `=` outside the final padding position may also move from accepted-by-regex to rejected-by-regex. Conversely, an R6 empty string is matched by the R6 regex but not the R4 regex, creating a down-conversion problem when the empty value is meaningful or required by a containing element. Strict parsers, generated regex validators, schema tests, and import pipelines are the most likely places to observe the change.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Before R6 validation, normalize legacy base64Binary strings by removing insignificant whitespace only after confirming the payload decodes successfully, then re-encode canonically. Do not blindly strip or rewrite values that fail base64 decoding; quarantine them for manual or source-system review because invalid padding may indicate corrupted content. Down-conversion tooling should decide how to handle R6 empty values: omit when the containing element allows absence, use an extension/profile-specific convention when absence is not equivalent, or reject with an explicit error.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The stricter R6 regex was probably avoidable in the narrow backward-compatibility sense: R6 could have continued accepting whitespace and loose padding while recommending canonical output. However, that would preserve known validation ambiguity and allow malformed encodings. The chosen regex improves conformance precision but imposes a real cleanup step for legacy R4 instances.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm against the rendered R6 datatype narrative or ballot change notes whether whitespace rejection is intentional for all serializations. Some implementations may already normalize base64 before applying the regex, which would reduce observed breakage but not change the computable StructureDefinition delta.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The material change is a computable constraint on the normative `base64Binary.value` primitive: R6 rejects whitespace-separated or line-wrapped lexical forms that the R4 regex accepted, and it also rejects some padding placements that R4's regex did not exclude. A strict validator, generated model check, import pipeline, or test fixture that accepted an R4 value such as a wrapped `Attachment.data`, `Binary.data`, or `Signature.data` string can fail after moving to R6 even though the element path, cardinality, and underlying FHIRPath type did not change. Tightening padding is a reasonable conformance goal, but removing all whitespace tolerance from a normative primitive looks worth renewed standards review because legitimate R4-era payloads can be normalized without changing the decoded bytes.
keyEvidence: R4 and R6 keep `base64Binary.value` at 0..1 with FHIRPath `System.String`; the local compatibility issue is the regex, not type or cardinality.
Anchored regex checks show `QUJD\nRA==` and `====` match the R4 regex but not the R6 regex, while the empty string matches R6 but not R4.
R4 package usage includes binary-bearing paths such as `Attachment.data`, `Binary.data`, and `Signature.data`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 `base64Binary` is normative, with normative status also visible in the local StructureDefinition/maturity data. That raises the justification burden for a hard validator-visible tightening, especially for a primitive used by many resources; it does not make every cleanup impermissible, but it pushes this from a routine cleanup to a change that should be reconsidered.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4-valid lexical values with whitespace or non-terminal padding can fail R6 validation. There is also R6-to-R4 loss at the regex level because R6 permits an empty lexical value that R4's regex did not match.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A plausible partial base-design alternative exists: preserve acceptance of insignificant whitespace around complete base64 quanta, enforce terminal padding, and state or warn that producers SHOULD emit canonical no-whitespace base64. That would preserve many legitimate R4 payloads while still rejecting malformed padding. The tradeoff is continued duplicate lexical forms for the same bytes, with possible canonicalization, signature, and string-comparison complications; those tradeoffs are real, but for a normative primitive they are not enough to dismiss the alternative without renewed review.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and alternative judgment. I agree this is a high-confidence hard instance break and that the alternative is partial rather than a clean preservation of every R4-valid string. I weigh the normative stability expectation and the modest whitespace-tolerant transition option more heavily, so I would mark it `Revisit` rather than treating the stricter regex as simply probably justified.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, status, abstract flag, and specialization derivation are stable. The baseDefinition change is deliberately excluded as an inherited primitive hierarchy concern.
The local snapshot still contains `base64Binary`, `base64Binary.id`, `base64Binary.extension`, and `base64Binary.value`; no local element was added, removed, renamed, split, or merged.
`base64Binary.value` remains `0..1`; inherited `id` and `extension` cardinalities also appear unchanged but are not counted as local findings.
`base64Binary.value` remains `http://hl7.org/fhirpath/System.String` with FHIR type extension `base64Binary`. The only local type-adjacent delta is the regex extension reported as a value constraint.
`base64Binary` is a primitive datatype and has no reference targets.
No terminology bindings are present on the assigned primitive value element.
No local invariant was added or removed on `base64Binary.value`. Inherited `ele-1` and `ext-1` details are out of scope; the regex extension change is reported separately as a value constraint.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value is present in either version.
`isModifier` remains false for the root, inherited children, and value element.
No local slicing is defined on `base64Binary.value` in either version.

The root definition and comment remain semantically the same: a stream of bytes, base64 encoded. Metadata description and publisher wording changed, but no local semantic tightening beyond the regex was found.
The representation of `base64Binary.value` remains `xmlAttr` and the JSON primitive representation is unchanged. The lexical serialization regex changed and is covered by the material finding.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds type-characteristics metadata `has-size`
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/structuredefinition-type-characteristics` with value `has-size`. This is metadata about the datatype's capabilities and does not by itself invalidate R4 instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Code generators or UI tooling that consumes R6 type characteristics may expose size-related behavior for `base64Binary`; this is additive metadata rather than a required instance shape change.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 changes primitive datatypes, including `base64Binary`, to specialize from `PrimitiveType` rather than directly from `Element`. Per the scope rule, class-hierarchy and inherited primitive behavior should be assessed in the PrimitiveType/DataType report, not duplicated here.

Inherited `ele-1`, Element child wording, and related XPath/source changes appear in the snapshots but are base-artifact concerns. They may affect validators globally and should be handled by the Element/Extension analyses.
